result: Arabidopsis CME follows the constant curvature model and generates predominantly hexagonal basket-type vesicles with a mean diameter of ~60 nm. Ultrastructural analysis using metal replica SEM revealed CCPs at various developmental stages with constant radius of curvature, absence of large flat lattices, and predominantly hexagonal basket structures (60%). Live TIRF-M imaging showed intensity profiles consistent with constant curvature model, with short maturation phase (17.8±8%) and longer assembly phase (42±5%).
evaluation: Claims C2, C3, C40-C66, C125-C126 collectively provide strong converging evidence from both ultrastructural (SEM) and live imaging (TIRF-M) approaches. The en face surface-view analysis demonstrating constant radius of curvature across developmental stages (C55, C56, C57), combined with intensity profile analysis showing phase segregation characteristic of constant curvature (C64, C65, C66), and the absence of large flat lattices (C52, C53) all support the constant curvature model. The hexagonal basket predominance (60%, C47) and size measurements (C43, C44, C45, C58) are well-documented with appropriate sample sizes.

result: Plant CME is faster and generates larger vesicles than yeast systems, with bona fide CME events having lifetimes of 42s in roots and 33s in hypocotyls. Statistical modeling of 149,162 CLC2 tracks identified three populations, with the longest-lived population (42s, 43.9% of total) confirmed as bona fide CME through dual-channel imaging with TPLATE and AP2 adaptors. This represents organ-specific regulation and is faster than yeast CME (75-135s) while producing larger vesicles (60nm vs 36nm in yeast).
evaluation: Claims C4, C5, C67-C76, C128, C130, C136, C151 provide robust quantitative evidence through large-scale automated tracking (149,162 tracks, C67), statistical modeling with appropriate model selection (C69), and independent validation through dual-channel imaging with multiple markers (C72, C73). The comparison with yeast is well-supported by citations (C130, C136). The discovery of organ-specific differences (C75, C76) is based on direct measurements in different tissues. Sample sizes are adequate and statistical approaches are appropriate.

result: Actin is dispensable for CME events at the plasma membrane in plants. Multiple lines of evidence show: (1) no actin enrichment at CCPs by SEM and TIRF-M (C82, C83, C84), (2) no effect of actin perturbation (LatB, Jasp) on CCP formation, CME kinetics, lifetime distributions, or developmental phases (C86, C87, C88), (3) continued internalization of multiple cargos (FM4-64, FLS2, PIN2) after actin disruption (C89, C90, C92), and (4) absence of type I myosin in plants (C133).
evaluation: Claims C6, C81-C93, C133-C134, C152 provide comprehensive evidence through multiple complementary approaches: ultrastructural analysis (SEM), live imaging (TIRF-M), pharmacological perturbation (LatB, Jasp), and cargo internalization assays. The lack of actin accumulation at CME sites is demonstrated by both SEM (C82) and TIRF-M (C83, C84). Quantitative analysis shows no significant changes in lifetime distributions, density, or developmental phases after actin perturbation (C87, C88), with appropriate statistical testing. Multiple cargo internalization assays (C89, C90, C92) and positive control with AUXILIN-LIKE2 (C91) strengthen the conclusion. This contradicts the prevailing paradigm but is well-supported by the data.

result: Actin plays a unique role in post-endocytic trafficking by mediating EE/TGN dynamics, collecting CCVs, and cargo sorting. Actin perturbation causes complete halt of GA and EE/TGN dynamics with local aggregations (C98), while FM4-64 still reaches aggregated endosomes (C99). However, cargo sorting is defective, with PIN2 mislocalization to aggregated late endosomes (C100). Live imaging shows spatial-temporal correlation between actin subsidiary filaments and CCV disappearance (C103), CCVs attached to actin filaments (C105), and EE/TGN picking up CCVs (C106, C107).
evaluation: Claims C7, C94-C108, C138-C140, C153 provide strong evidence for actin's role in post-endocytic events through multiple approaches. The halt of EE/TGN dynamics after actin perturbation (C98) is clearly demonstrated by imaging. The endosomal pick-up analysis (C107) provides unbiased quantitative evidence with significant increase in CCV tracks ending in endosomal ROIs (p=0.0066 for root, p=0.0223 for hypocotyl). The observation that FM4-64 reaches aggregated endosomes (C99) while PIN2 is mislocalized (C100) suggests actin is required for specific cargo sorting rather than general membrane delivery. The spatial-temporal correlations (C103, C105, C106) are supported by live imaging and SEM data.

result: Actin-mediated directional endosome movement actively promotes CME events at the PM. There is strong spatio-temporal relationship between actin filament dynamics and CME events (C141), and significant correlation between CME termination and EE/TGN movement passing below the PM (C142). The endosomal pick-up analysis shows increased rate of CME when mobile EE passes by (C154), suggesting an active role of endosome movement in mediating CME.
evaluation: Claims C9, C141-C143, C154-C155 are supported by the endosomal pick-up analysis showing significant increase in CCV tracks ending when endosomes pass by (referenced in C107, C142). The spatio-temporal correlations are demonstrated through live imaging (C141). However, while the correlation is well-established, the mechanistic understanding of how endosome movement 'actively promotes' CME could benefit from additional experiments. The data support a correlation and suggest an active role, but direct causation is inferred rather than definitively proven.

result: Internalized vesicles display strongly delayed and sequential uncoating. Many CCVs retain their clathrin coat until reaching EE/TGN (C113), with both clathrin and adaptor retained until fusion (C115). After fusion, adaptor disappears but uncoating occurs immediately before or during fusion (C116). For CCVs trafficked longer in cytosol, sequential loss of adaptor before clathrin is observed (C119, C120), occurring in majority of cases (18/20 CCVs, C121). This is supported by TEM showing partially uncoated CCVs in cytosol (C122) and SEM showing partially coated CCVs fused to endosomal membranes (C117).
evaluation: Claims C10, C113-C124, C150, C156 provide strong evidence through dual-channel TIRF-M imaging tracking both clathrin (CLC2) and adaptor (TPLATE) simultaneously. The observation of sequential uncoating in 18/20 CCVs (C121) provides quantitative support, though the sample size is relatively small. The findings are corroborated by independent ultrastructural evidence from both TEM (C122) and SEM (C117) showing partially uncoated vesicles. The delayed uncoating is a novel finding that contradicts established models in other systems (C150), making it a significant discovery. The mechanistic details of the uncoating process are well-documented through time-lapse imaging.

result: Plant CME mechanism evolved independently during the autonomous rise of multicellularity in eukaryotes. Multiple unique features distinguish plant CME: actin-independent membrane bending (C152), organ-specific regulation (C129), differential clathrin recycling (C131), and potentially multiple membrane bending mechanisms (C127). These features, combined with the unique post-endocytic roles of actin and delayed uncoating, suggest independent evolution despite conserved molecular components (C158).
evaluation: Claims C11, C127, C129, C131, C137, C152, C158 represent the overarching evolutionary interpretation of the findings. This conclusion is well-supported by the multiple unique features documented in the manuscript: actin-independence (contrary to yeast), faster kinetics with larger vesicles, organ-specific regulation, and delayed sequential uncoating. The inference of independent evolution (C11, C158) is reasonable given the constellation of unique features, though it remains an interpretation rather than direct evidence. The speculation about co-evolution with multicellularity (C137) is appropriately presented as a possibility. The claim is supported by the cumulative weight of evidence showing mechanistic differences from both yeast and mammalian systems.

result: Background and motivation claims establishing that CME is the major endocytic route in plants, that plant CME is poorly characterized, and that the field has relied on inferences from mammalian and yeast systems. These claims establish the knowledge gap and rationale for the study.
evaluation: Claims C1, C12-C39 are primarily background knowledge claims supported by appropriate citations to previous literature. These establish the context and motivation for the study. The claims about CME being the major route in plants (C1, C15), conservation of components (C20-C25), and differences in actin requirement between yeast and mammals (C27-C31) are well-supported by citations. The identification of knowledge gaps (C18, C26, C34, C35, C38) appropriately motivates the study.

result: Technical and interpretive observations about CCS populations and intracellular structures. Resin embedding was less efficient than metal replica (C42), size differences may be due to hexagon numbers (C46), multiple fused CCSs are found on intracellular membranes (C48), and these structures may be EE/TGN or secretory vesicles (C49, C50, C51).
evaluation: Claims C42, C46, C48-C51 are methodological observations and speculations. The comparison of techniques (C42) is based on direct observation. The speculation about hexagon numbers affecting size (C46) is appropriately cited to theoretical work. The observations of intracellular CCS arrangements (C48) are documented in figures. The interpretations about identity of intracellular structures (C49-C51) are appropriately presented as possibilities with citations to previous work.

result: Comparative and contextual claims about CME in other systems and technical considerations. These include observations about large mobile clathrin structures being EE/TGN (C61), comparisons with mammalian intensity profiles (C63), background on actin's role in yeast/mammals (C77-C80), uncoating in other systems (C109-C112, C144-C149), technical notes about CLC2 localization (C132), and statements about the value of multicellular model systems (C157).
evaluation: Claims C61, C63, C77-C80, C109-C112, C132-C133, C135-C136, C144-C149, C157 are primarily comparative, contextual, or technical observations. Most are supported by appropriate citations to previous literature. The observation about mobile clathrin structures (C61) is supported by imaging data. The technical note about CLC2 localization (C132) acknowledges a limitation. The comparative claims about other systems (C77-C80, C109-C112, C144-C149) are well-cited. These claims provide important context but are not primary findings.
